content: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is defined as the presence of at least 10^5 colony-forming units of bacteria per milliliter of urine in a clean, midstream urine sample, without any symptoms of a urinary tract infection. Studies indicate that the prevalence of asymptomatic bacteriuria during pregnancy ranges from 2% to 10%, depending on socioeconomic factors. Pregnant women, those with anatomical or functional urinary tract abnormalities, individuals of lower socioeconomic status, those with anemia, sickle cell trait, diabetes mellitus, or HIV infection are at higher risk for asymptomatic bacteriuria. The urinary tract in pregnant women has several defense mechanisms to prevent infections. These include the downward flow of urine, the protective vaginal flora, and the glycosaminoglycan-containing mucin layer in the bladder, which acts as a barrier. Urine also contains antibacterial substances such as urea, organic acids, salts, and Tamm-Horsfall protein, which traps bacteria for elimination. Secretory immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA) and the complement system further enhance protection. However, during pregnancy, these defenses can be compromised due to anatomical and hormonal changes. The growing uterus can obstruct the ureters, and elevated progesterone levels relax smooth muscles, leading to urinary stasis. This stasis, along with increased glucose and amino acid excretion in urine, creates an environment conducive to bacterial growth. Most urinary tract infections in pregnancy are caused by bacteria, primarily Escherichia coli (E. coli), which accounts for 80% of cases. Other organisms, such as Staphylococcus saprophyticus and enterococci, are less common. These bacteria often originate from the bowel, colonize the perineum, and ascend to the urinary tract. Sexual activity and catheterization can facilitate this process. Hematogenous spread is rare but may occur in immunocompromised individuals. The diagnosis of asymptomatic bacteriuria is made by isolating bacteria with a colony count of at least 10^5 organisms per milliliter in a clean-catch urine sample. Proper cleaning of the vulva before sample collection is essential to avoid contamination. Asymptomatic bacteriuria is clinically significant because it increases the risk of urinary tract infections, pyelonephritis (kidney infection), and renal impairment during pregnancy. If left untreated, up to 40% of pregnant women with asymptomatic bacteriuria may develop urinary tract infections, and 25% to 30% may progress to acute pyelonephritis. Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria can reduce the risk of pyelonephritis by approximately 75%. Asymptomatic bacteriuria has been linked to adverse pregnancy outcomes, including preterm delivery, miscarriage, and pregnancy-induced hypertension. Treating this condition may mitigate these risks. There is emerging evidence suggesting that cranberry products may play a role in managing asymptomatic bacteriuria during pregnancy. Cranberries contain proanthocyanidins, which exhibit anti-adhesion properties against both antibiotic-sensitive and resistant strains of E. coli. However, the optimal dosage, duration, and form of cranberry products (juice, capsules, or tablets) for use during pregnancy remain unclear. Cranberries are composed of approximately 80% water and 10% carbohydrates, with the remaining 10% consisting of organic acids such as ascorbic acid, malic acid, salicylic acid, oxalic acid, benzoic acid, and citric acid. These acids contribute to the sour taste of cranberries, often necessitating the addition of sugar to cranberry juice for palatability. Cranberries also contain catechins, flavonoids (including proanthocyanidins), and other phenolic compounds. Among these, proanthocyanidins are considered the most active in preventing bacterial adhesion. Vaccinium fruits, including cranberries, are among the richest dietary sources of proanthocyanidins. The therapeutic dose of cranberry juice is estimated to be at least 300 mL daily. Some studies suggest that consuming one glass of cranberry juice in the morning and evening may be beneficial. However, standardizing the therapeutic dosage has been challenging, making it difficult to compare different regimens. Adverse effects of cranberries are rare but may include gastrointestinal discomfort and a bitter taste. Cranberries do not kill bacteria or sterilize the urinary tract. Instead, they prevent bacteria from adhering to uroepithelial cells, thereby reducing the likelihood of urinary tract infections. Proanthocyanidins in cranberries reach peak concentrations in the urinary tract within three to six hours after ingestion. The anti-adhesion effects are particularly effective against uropathogenic E. coli, which possess adhesins that facilitate attachment to uroepithelial cells. The A-type linkage in cranberry proanthocyanidins enhances their anti-adhesion activity. These compounds bind to bacterial lipopolysaccharides, a key component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, further inhibiting adhesion. Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials have demonstrated the ability of cranberries to inhibit E. coli adherence to uroepithelial cells. Other studies suggest that vaginal fluid may influence bacterial adherence, and nitric oxide generated under mildly acidic conditions may also contribute to the antimicrobial effects of cranberries. Cranberries may even prevent the adhesion of antibiotic-resistant E. coli strains. The increasing prevalence of antibiotic resistance has renewed interest in cranberries as a potential treatment for urinary tract infections in women with asymptomatic bacteriuria. Asymptomatic bacteriuria is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes such as pyelonephritis, preterm labor, low birth weight, maternal anemia, and hypertension. Treating this condition reduces these risks. While cranberries have shown promise in treating asymptomatic bacteriuria, their efficacy in pregnant women remains uncertain. A randomized clinical trial found a higher frequency of pyelonephritis in pregnant women taking cranberries compared to those who did not, possibly due to pregnancy-related hormonal effects and urinary stasis. Further research is needed to evaluate the role of cranberries in managing asymptomatic bacteriuria during pregnancy.
